title: Scientists Confirm an Ancient Asteroid Hit the North Sea
summary:
About 43 to 46 million years ago, an asteroid crashed into the area now covered by the North Sea, sending up a tsunami more than 100 meters (330 feet) high. Now scientists say they finally have proof.

The impact left behind the Silverpit Crater, which lies about 700 meters below the seabed, roughly 80 miles off the coast of Yorkshire, England. The crater is about three kilometers wide and is surrounded by a 20-kilometer-wide ring of cracks in the rock.

Scientists discovered the crater in 2002. It has a round shape and a raised peak in the middle, like other impact craters. But some geologists thought it could have formed in other ways, such as from moving underground salt or a collapse caused by volcanoes. In 2009, geologists even held a vote on the question, and most rejected the asteroid idea.

A team led by Dr. Uisdean Nicholson of Heriot-Watt University in Edinburgh has now settled the debate. The researchers used new seismic images, which use sound waves to see layers of rock underground. They also studied rock pieces collected from a nearby oil well, and ran computer simulations of the crash.

The key clue was tiny crystals of "shocked" quartz and feldspar found at the same depth as the crater floor. These crystals have a pattern that can only be made by extreme pressure, like that of a space rock smashing into Earth.

"We were exceptionally lucky to find these," Nicholson said, calling it a "needle-in-a-haystack" effort. The study, published in Nature Communications, makes Silverpit one of the few confirmed impact craters on Earth.
why_it_matters: Confirming impact craters helps scientists understand how often big space rocks have struck Earth and what effects, like giant tsunamis, they can cause.

keywords.explanation: An asteroid is a rocky object that orbits the Sun and is smaller than a planet.
A tsunami is a series of huge ocean waves usually caused by a sudden push of water, such as an earthquake or impact.
Seismic images are pictures of underground rock layers made by sending sound waves into the ground and recording the echoes.
Quartz is a common, hard mineral found in many kinds of rock.
Simulations are computer models that recreate how something might have happened.
Impact craters are bowl-shaped holes made when an object from space smashes into a planet or moon.

background_read: Earth has been hit by asteroids and comets throughout its history, but erosion, oceans and moving rock have erased or buried most of the craters.
Scientists confirm an impact crater by finding evidence that only an enormous collision can create, such as minerals changed by extreme shock pressure.
Seismic imaging lets geologists study buried structures, like Silverpit, by sending sound waves through rock and recording how they bounce back.
Before this study, some geologists thought salt movement or volcanic collapse could explain Silverpit's shape.
